implementation_notes: Node and browser JavaScript are single-threaded and I/O-bound, so the bulkhead is an outstanding-work bound rather than a thread bound: p-limit(n) returns a limiter that queues tasks above n concurrent executions and bottleneck adds reservoirs and priorities; create one limiter per dependency so a slow dependency's backlog cannot grow behind another's. Rejection is not built in - the queue is unbounded - so bound pending work yourself and use AbortSignal and timeouts so queued tasks can be abandoned; a worker_threads pool per dependency remains the right tool when the work is CPU-bound.

variants.name: p-limit / bottleneck limiter per dependency
variants.implementation_notes: Node and browser JavaScript are single-threaded and I/O-bound, so the bulkhead is an outstanding-work bound rather than a thread bound: p-limit(n) returns a limiter that queues tasks above n concurrent executions and bottleneck adds reservoirs and priorities; create one limiter per dependency so a slow dependency's backlog cannot grow behind another's. Rejection is not built in - the queue is unbounded - so bound pending work yourself and use AbortSignal and timeouts so queued tasks can be abandoned; a worker_threads pool per dependency remains the right tool when the work is CPU-bound.
pitfalls: p-limit's queue is unbounded: a stalled dependency accumulates promises until memory pressure kills the process, so bound pending work or abort queued tasks.
A limiter shared across all dependencies recreates the coupling, and one created inside a request handler re-creates the pool per request.
Promises cannot be cancelled: limiters retain pending closures, so pass AbortSignal and time out inside the task, not only around the await.
fetch and undici keep their own connection pools, so a limiter of 8 does not bound sockets unless the agent or pool is configured too.

variants.name: per-origin connection cap (http.Agent maxSockets)
variants.implementation_notes: Socket-level bulkhead: give each dependency its own http.Agent with maxSockets (and maxFreeSockets), so requests queue inside that agent only and the resource that actually fails first under overload - sockets and file descriptors - is bounded per dependency. It composes with a promise-slot limiter, which bounds application work rather than sockets, but it is not a substitute: the agent queue is unbounded, so pair it with a request timeout or a queue bound.
pitfalls: The agent's queue is unbounded, so without a request timeout saturation shows up as growing latency instead of rejection.
maxSockets is per host:port, so it does not isolate two dependencies that share the same host and port.
HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one socket, so maxSockets does not bound concurrent streams; use the client's stream limits instead.
Keep-alive agents hold free sockets per dependency; tune maxFreeSockets or descriptors accumulate.
